html:
Great Zimbabwe was a stone-walled city in the hills of south-eastern Zimbabwe, near Masvingo, and the capital of a kingdom of ancestral Shona people. People settled there from around 1000, building went on from the 1000s into the 1400s, and it was the seat of a state from the 1200s.

Its walls are granite blocks fitted without mortar. The largest ruin, the Great Enclosure, has curving walls up to about 11 m high and a solid conical tower inside. The city spread over about 7 square kilometres. Older estimates put its peak population near 20,000; recent work suggests no more than 10,000.

Its wealth came from cattle and from gold. Gold and ivory went down to the coast, where traders of the Swahili city-states shipped them across the Indian Ocean. Glass beads, Persian pottery and Chinese porcelain found at the site show how far that Indian Ocean trade reached. The state followed the earlier Kingdom of Mapungubwe to the south.

In the 1400s the city declined, perhaps because soils and grazing wore out and trade routes moved. Power shifted north to Mutapa and west to Khami.

From the late 1800s, European writers claimed that foreigners such as the Phoenicians must have built it, and the government of white-ruled Rhodesia later pressed that view. Archaeologists showed in 1905 and again in 1929 that it was African work. When the country won majority rule in 1980 it took the name Zimbabwe from the site, and the soapstone birds found there became a national emblem.
